sections.h2: Does every Palm Bay house run on city water and sewer?
sections.html:
No. The Utilities Department's service area covers a large share of the city but not all of it, and thousands of homes still rely on septic tanks or private wells. The city's own count is more than 32,000 septic systems and 12,000 drinking water wells.

That fact shapes a Palm Bay sale more than most sellers expect. A buyer's lender, inspector and insurer will all ask what the house drains into and where its water comes from, so settle the answer before listing. The city offers an interactive map: type the full address and it shows whether lines are in place.

The utility is run as an enterprise fund, which the city says means it takes no property tax money and lives on customer revenue. Rates are adjusted every October 1, and a formal rate study happens every five years or when warranted.

sections.h2: What is Palm Bay's mandatory connection rule?
sections.html:
It is an ordinance, approved November 2, 2023, that requires developed properties with city lines readily available to hook up. The city says state law, section 381.00655(1)(a) of the Florida Statutes, governs mandatory sewer connection.

As of October 1, 2023, the city counted about 1,066 developed parcels with sewer available but not connected, called SANC, and 2,344 with water available but not connected, called WANC. Of those, 289 have neither service.

  • The city notifies owners in writing, in phases that began in summer 2024.
  • Each owner then has one year from the date of the notice to connect.
  • Households in the active phase receive information on septic-to-sewer funding eligibility.
  • Eligible owners work with a pre-approved contractor, and the funding source reimburses the contractor after the agreement is met.
  • A sewer account must be opened, and a $100 deposit may apply.

If a notice has arrived for your address, treat the one-year clock as part of the sale.

sections.h2: What does connecting to city water or sewer cost in Palm Bay?
sections.html:
The city bases its published figures on a standard 80-foot lot and says fees can change, so confirm your own amount with Customer Care at (321) 952-3420.

Owner-occupied residential accounts can set up a connection payment agreement for up to five years, by appointment. A fixed $10 monthly service charge is added. The meter and the deposit cannot be financed.

sections.h2: How does a septic-to-sewer switch actually work in Palm Bay?
sections.html:
It runs through the utility, the Health Department and the Building Division, in that order. Knowing the order helps a seller judge how long a switch would take before closing.

  1. Check availability on the city map and confirm costs with Customer Care.
  2. Complete a residential application and pay the connection charges.
  3. The utility issues a work order to locate the clean-out or tap-in point for the sewer lateral.
  4. A septic contractor or the owner obtains a permit from the county Department of Health, and a city building permit is also needed.
  5. The contractor abandons the tank while an environmental health inspector watches.
  6. A plumber connects the lateral to the house, ideally before the tank is abandoned so service is never interrupted.

The city recommends hiring a licensed septic contractor and a Florida licensed, insured plumber. The Building Division is in the City Hall Annex at 120 Malabar Road SE, phone (321) 953-8924.

sections.h2: How should a Palm Bay seller handle a septic or well house?
sections.html:
Decide whether to connect first or to sell as is, and tell buyers which one you chose. Both are workable. Cash offers tend to discount for the switching cost, while a financed buyer's lender may want repairs finished.

  • Pull the city map result for your address and save a copy.
  • Keep any mandatory connection notice, since its one-year window passes to the next owner.
  • Gather septic pumping and well records if you have them.
  • Ask Customer Care about payment agreements, which apply to owner-occupied accounts.

Selling as is to a renovator skips the hookup work altogether. Whichever way you go, put the water and sewer facts in writing so they are never a surprise at inspection.

sections.h2: What did the November flood add to a Palm Bay sale?
sections.html:
It added documentation and, for some owners, help. The city's flood event page describes waived permit fees for residential flood repairs, a damage reporting form run through Brevard County Emergency Management, and a Disaster Relief Program for owners who meet homestead, payment and income tests.

Owners with a National Flood Insurance Program policy need a substantial damage inspection as part of the claim and before permits. The Building Department asks owners to call (321) 953-8924 before starting work.

A house that took on water can still be sold. Keep photos, estimates and permits together, since a buyer's insurer will ask. If you would rather skip repairs, an as-is cash sale shifts that work to the buyer.

sections.h2: Which flood zone papers help a Palm Bay listing?
sections.html:
Lenders check the flood zone on every purchase, so having paper ready speeds things along. The city's flood information page points to a few useful items.

  • Elevation certificates: the Building Department keeps floodplain review copies with FEMA Elevation Certificates for homes built since 1993.
  • Map history: a FEMA map that took effect March 17, 2014 moved about 2,000 structures out of the Special Flood Hazard Area, and those owners may qualify for a Preferred Risk policy.
  • Insurance discount: the city reports a Community Rating System rating of 7, described as a 15 percent reduction in federal flood insurance premiums.

Mortgages backed by federal agencies require flood coverage inside the hazard area, so a buyer will price that policy into the offer.

sections.h2: Which Palm Bay permit rules catch sellers off guard?
sections.html:
The city's permit FAQ lists more jobs than people assume, including fences, sheds, re-roofing, window and door replacement, air conditioner change-outs, electrical, plumbing, gas work and generators.

Work begun without a permit risks a penalty reaching four times the fee. Residential permits average 14 working days for approval, and applications go through an online portal. An owner-builder permit is allowed only when the property will not be sold or leased for a year, which matters for anyone planning a quick flip. Open permits and unpermitted work come up at inspection, so close them out before listing.

sections.h2: How do Brevard County taxes and deed costs fit a Palm Bay sale?
sections.html:
The Brevard County Property Appraiser values property each January 1, and bills arrive in November with a 4% discount that shrinks to 1% by February. Unpaid bills are delinquent after April 1, and a certificate sale follows by June 1.

Homestead reduces taxable value by up to $50,000, and the new owner is reassessed after a sale. Deed stamps are 70 cents per $100 in Brevard, collected by the clerk at recording. Ask the title agent for a draft settlement statement early so stamps, recording fees and prorated taxes are clear.

faqs.q: How do I know if my Palm Bay home can connect to city sewer?
faqs.a: Enter your full address in the interactive map on the Palm Bay Utilities service availability page, or call Customer Care at (321) 952-3420 to confirm.

faqs.q: What is the deadline to connect once Palm Bay sends a notice?
faqs.a: Twelve months after the written notification, under the mandatory connection ordinance approved November 2, 2023.

faqs.q: Can I finance a Palm Bay water or sewer hookup?
faqs.a: Yes for owner-occupied residential accounts. Connection payment agreements run up to five years, with a $10 monthly service charge, and the meter and deposit are excluded.

faqs.q: Are Palm Bay permit fees waived for flood repairs?
faqs.a: The city's flood event page says the Building Department waives permit fees for residential flood-related repairs. Call (321) 953-8924 before starting work.

faqs.q: Does a Palm Bay seller's homestead savings pass to the buyer?
faqs.a: No. A sale triggers reassessment at just value, so the buyer does not receive the seller's capped assessment.
